extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral and political philosophy (general educated readership; scholars of ethics and Schopenhauer)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains principles of moral psychology, ethics, and the theory of the State (aims of government, rights, property) as presented in a philosophical treatise. Focus is on conceptual definitions and normative claims about willing, repentance, rights, and the justification of political institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclination (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Inclination is every strong susceptibility of the will for motives of a certain kind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic definitional criterion distinguishing types of motivational states; serves as the ground for understanding passions and moral responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion (definition and features)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Passion is an inclination so strong that the motives which excite it exercise a power over the will, which is stronger than that of every possible motive that can oppose them; thus its mastery over the will becomes absolute, and consequently with reference to it the will is passive or suffering."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passions rarely reach the full degree of this definition; counter-motives may still partially restrict them. Passions make the will effectively passive and explain diminished intellectual freedom prior to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion (definition and relation to passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The emotion is just as irresistible, but yet only a passing excitement of the will, by a motive which receives its power from appearing suddenly and excluding counter-effects; it consists of an idea which completely obscures all others by its excessive vividness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotion differs from passion in being transient and arising from vivid ideas that temporarily abolish intellectual freedom. The text characterises the relation as 'the emotion is related to the passion as delirium to madness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral repentance (conditions and explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral repentance arises when, before an act, inclination prevented the intellect from fully contemplating counter-motives, but after the act those motives are neutralised and the intellect recognises that the action was not fully in accord with the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repentance is explained via the interplay of will and intellect: passions/emotions suppress intellectual consideration pre-act; post-act the intellect perceives counter-motives (consequences) and recognises lack of full intellectual freedom. Examples: murders driven by revenge/jealousy/avarice; marriages entered from passion that later reveal lost independence and personal-interest counter-motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of character (σωφροσυνη)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonableness (σωφροσυνη) opposed to passionateness: consists in that the will never overpowers the intellect so as to prevent it from distinctly and fully presenting motives (in the abstract) and their concrete imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trait depends on a suitable relation between will and intellect—either a mild will or strong intellect—so that intellect can fulfil its function of presenting counter-motives and prevent actions driven by unexamined inclination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weeping springs from sympathy with oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: Weeping (in certain cases) arises from sympathy the object of which is one's own self — e.g., remembrance of a brighter past contrasts with present wretchedness and evokes tears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with Ulysses in the Odyssey and other classical examples; supports a psychological account of affect as reflective sympathy rather than direct immediate sorrow about the present state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics concerns willing and the individual (scope of ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics is concerned not with actions and their results, but with willing; and willing itself takes place only in the individual. Therefore moral evaluation properly focuses on the individual, not on nations or collective abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument given against views that make the material of ethics the conduct of nations; mass phenomena are phenomonal abstractions and lack the moral 'content' that individuals contain as embodiments of the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right exists independently of the State
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who deny that there is a right apart from the State confound the means for enforcing the right with the right itself: the right exists independently, though the State insures its protection; by force it can be suppressed, never abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes ontological status of right from institutional enforcement; frames State as protective institution rather than originator of right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims of the State — (1) Outward protection / law of nations
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Outward protection: protection which may be needful against lifeless forces of nature, wild beasts, or other nations; since nations often profess defensive rather than aggressive relations, they recognise the law of nations — described as natural law in the sphere between nation and nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law of nations is practical morality between states where positive law cannot reach; its tribunal is public opinion. Emphasises the State's role in collective defence and international morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims of the State — (2) Protection within (security of private right)
rubrics_metrics.description: (2) Protection within: protection of members of a State against each other, securing private right by maintaining an honest state of things so that concentrated social forces protect each individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This internal protection creates the appearance that all are just and unwilling to injure others; it is the reason for civil law and institutions securing private rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims of the State — (3) Protection against the protector / separation of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: (3) Protection against the protector: the need to guard citizens from those entrusted with protection; best achieved by dividing the protective power into separate legislature, judicature, and executive, each independent of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text further argues that monarchy has the virtue of neutralising egoism by concentrating immunity, wealth, and status in one person so that he may practise justice disinterestedly; monarchy should be hereditary (not elective) to prevent rivals and align the monarch's interest with state welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property arises through labour
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of property arises only through the expenditure of labour upon things; property is 'as it were only embodied work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by contemporary (to the text) appeals and citations (e.g., Quincey Adams) and used against communistic critiques; grounds legitimacy of property in personal labour and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pantheism undermines ethics (ethical consequence of metaphysical views)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the world is a theophany (pantheism), then everything man or brute does is equally divine and excellent; nothing can be censurable, and nothing more praiseworthy than the rest; thus there is no ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an argument against pantheism: ethics collapses if moral distinctions are absorbed into a single divine substance. The text contrasts this with the author's doctrine identifying the force in nature with the will, thereby preserving a moral ordering grounded in the will rather than an undifferentiated divinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of philosophical inquiry (doctrine reaches a boundary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy cannot answer all questions (would be the science of omniscience); the author's doctrine of the will to live reaches a limit beyond which reflection cannot penetrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges methodological humility: some problems remain despite the presented system; positions the ethics/ontology claims as reaching but not exceeding that limit.
